comments.text:
Hi, love your reviews — really top-notch, detailed stuff.

I'm a bit baffled by your LatencyMon results across the Legion Pro 7 lineup. In your 2025 tests (275HX, different GPU tiers) I'm seeing very different peak DPC numbers — one config came in around 463 µs, another around 830 µs. Then in your review of the new 2026 version (290HX Plus / RTX 5090), the peak DPC jumped to roughly 1,900 µs and LatencyMon actually flagged it as having trouble with real-time audio — worst result of the bunch, despite being the newest chip the problem is the same with 5070 12 GB GPU version.

A couple of things stood out that made me want to ask:

1. Is each unit tested with a clean Windows install, or the same OS install reused/updated across review units?
2. Are Vantage, RGB control software, and any power-management utilities uninstalled or disabled before the test, or left as shipped?
3. Is Windows Update / background telemetry disabled during the test window?
4. For the 290HX Plus unit specifically — I noticed the hard pagefault count was over 11,000, versus 400–500 on the earlier units. Any idea what drove that? It makes me wonder if something (indexing, updates, low free RAM at test time) was running in the background rather than it being a clean idle measurement.
5. Are all your LatencyMon runs done idle, right after boot, on AC power, same duration?

Not trying to nitpick — I'm genuinely trying to figure out if the 290HX Plus result reflects the platform (new BIOS/power management still maturing) or just test conditions on that particular run, since I'm deciding between these for audio production (Cubase) and DPC stability matters a lot for me. Would really appreciate knowing your test protocol so I can weigh the numbers properly. Thanks for the great content either way!

comments.text:
I have a 2025 Legion Pro 7i 275HX/5080/64GB DDR5, and it is an amazing laptop. Picked it up for $2500 new from BB around Christmastime. Kinda disappointing to see just the 290HX change, but impressive they get an additional hour of battery life out of it. This laptop is not great for doing remote work on when you're in a pinch unless its only for a couple of hours. 

Beyond that though, love this laptop. When I travel I take my 135W Lenovo GAN charger, and it works great. 

The key is also enabling Silent Performance mode, which very few reviewers seem to touch on (maybe I missed it here?). But that increases GPU power, and decreases CPU power & fan speed in silent mode. Using that with the 400W charger or 135W GAN charger seems to work well. Even with that, you must use the 400W charger to get "full" silent performance mode power. 

But it is pretty rare I even need to switch to Balance, let alone Max Performance to play the games I play. With Silent Performance disabled, you have more CPU power which makes more sense if you're doing more CPU-intensive tasks. But if you want extra GPU grunt, the 275HX, and I assume 290HX, do well with 60-65W power limitation and are quite efficient in that area. I didn't notice any performance degradation by "seat of the pants" measurements. YMMV, but well worth checking out if you own one of these amazing laptops.

Hopefully we can get back to more appropriate prices that make these more acquireable than they currently are, prices are disgusting.

comments.text:
Thanks for the update.  My use model is less about portability and more about convenience.  When I was in the corporate world, I was traveling 60,000 miles per year and a lightweight, minimalist laptop was key.  100% Microsoft Office use and similar loads -- minor, easy, no gaming.  I wanted light, portable, and minimalist.  As a home user, I am not looking for actual portability ... I'm not taking my laptop on cross-continental journeys.  I just want to be able to work and play on my couch, as opposed to a desk in an office ... and I want a hefty GPU that can handle gaming demands.

So, with that said, I appreciate huge 400W power bricks and design choices (e.g., heavier heat sinks and fans) that prioritize performance over portability.  Similarly, I don't care tons about battery life and performance caps when the power cord is disconnected.  Again, I'm just sitting on a couch with the PC still plugged in.

The one thing that keeps ringing true with Lenovo is that it does not throttle the laptop.  It allows massive amounts of power to both be supplied and used by the hardware.  While I understand that this becomes inconvenient when traveling from Denver to Tokyo, I am most interested in maximizing performance when I'm moving about my own home.

I'm currently living with an HP with a hardware defect, along with various hardware limitations.  I'm waiting (in summer 2026) for the Lenovo Pro 7i to become affordable to me, which basically means waiting a few months until Black Friday deals hit again. (i.e., that 7i 5080 is around $2,500 - $2,600 for the past few months in June 2026; the lowest price was in the 2025 holiday shopping months for around $2,000 - $2,1000.  I'm waiting for the 7i 5080 to again hit that ~$2000 price point. Wish me luck)

I appreciate your quick-hitting, data-driven approach to these videos.  No long narratives, I don't have to hear stories about what you had for breakfast, and so on. I'm using last year's black Lenovo Legion Pro 7 16IAX10H

For a machine that costs around €4,000, it simply doesn't feel premium at all. I have no complaints about the performance - the CPU and GPU are excellent - but the overall build quality, materials, and user experience are disappointing.

Here are my main issues:

• It attracts fingerprints everywhere, even on the keyboard keys, and some of them are surprisingly difficult to clean off.
• It constantly drains the battery even while plugged into the wall using the massive and mostly pointless 400W power brick.
• Lenovo's software is extremely buggy. You can't properly configure the RGB lighting, and despite contacting support, the issues were never fixed. It also frequently charges the battery above the 80% limit even when the charging threshold is enabled.
• The worst part is the audio. These are some of the worst laptop speakers I've ever heard. The sound quality is absolutely terrible. Even my phone sounds better than this expensive laptop.
• The OLED display is also a mixed bag. Lenovo's heavily advertised burn-in protection features will most likely stay disabled because they're incredibly annoying in daily use. For example, the screen keeps dimming while watching videos. In practice, the only protection you'll probably end up using is the Windows screen timeout. As I mentioned earlier, Lenovo's software is simply not reliable enough.
• The lack of both an SD card reader and a fingerprint scanner is frankly ridiculous

Before this, I owned an older Asus Zephyrus G16, and honestly it felt better in almost every way. It was a laptop that you actually wanted to pick up and use, and the speakers were fantastic. Unfortunately, I no longer trust Asus either because that laptop started developing hardware issues and gave me several technical problems.

That said, I wouldn't buy Lenovo again either. Paying a premium price just for a powerful CPU and GPU isn't enough for me. At this price point, the entire experience should feel premium, and the Legion 7 Pro simply doesn't.
